evidence.text: Phillips produces a variety of liquors such as Vodka, Gin, Rum, Canadian whisky, Brandy and many flavors of Schnapps.
evidence.title: Phillips Distilling Company

evidence.text: In recent years, Phillips has branched out beyond standard liquors with a variety of specialty drinks, such as Revel Stoke Spiced Whisky (the original spiced whisky), Gin-Ka (a combination of gin and vodka), Phillips Union Whiskey, the 100 proof series of Schnapps (Hot, Blue, and Root Beer), and vodka such as UV Vodka and the handcrafted and organic Prairie Vodka.

evidence.text: Proto-Norse (also called Proto-Scandinavian, Primitive Norse, Proto-Nordic, Ancient Nordic, Ancient Scandinavian, Old Nordic, Old Scandinavian, Proto-North Germanic, North Proto-Germanic or Common Scandinavian) was an Indo-European language spoken in Scandinavia that is thought to have evolved as a northern dialect of Proto-Germanic in the first centuries CE.

evidence.text: It evolved into the dialects of Old Norse at the beginning of the Viking Age in about 800, which later themselves evolved into modern North Germanic languages.

evidence.text: Afrikaans ( ) is a West Germanic language spoken in South Africa, Namibia and, to a lesser extent, Botswana and Zimbabwe.
evidence.title: Afrikaans

evidence.text: It evolved from the Dutch vernacular of South Holland (Hollandic dialect) spoken by the mainly Dutch settlers of what is now South Africa, where it gradually began to develop distinguishing characteristics in the course of the 18th century.

evidence.text: Hence, it is a daughter language of Dutch, and was previously referred to as "Cape Dutch" (a term also used to refer collectively to the early Cape settlers) or "kitchen Dutch" (a derogatory term used to refer to Afrikaans in its earlier days).

evidence.text: Suorva or Suorvadammen (the Suorva Dam) is a small settlement situated at the southern parts of Akkajaure, in Stora Sjöfallet National Park, Sweden.

evidence.text: Old Saxon, also known as Old Low German, was a Germanic language and the earliest recorded form of Low German (spoken nowadays in Northern Germany, the northeastern Netherlands, southern Denmark, the Americas and parts of Eastern Europe).
evidence.title: Old Saxon

evidence.text: It is a West Germanic language, closely related to the Anglo-Frisian languages.
evidence.title: Old Saxon

evidence.text: It has been documented from the 8th century until the 12th century, when it gradually evolved into Middle Low German.
evidence.title: Old Saxon

evidence.text: It was spoken throughout modern northwestern Germany, primarily in the coastal regions and in the eastern Netherlands by Saxons, a Germanic tribe who inhabited the region of Saxony.
evidence.title: Old Saxon

evidence.text: It partially shares Anglo-Frisian's (Old Frisian, Old English) Ingvaeonic nasal spirant law which sets it apart from Low Franconian and Irminonic languages, such as Dutch, Luxembourgish and German.
evidence.title: Old Saxon

evidence.text: The Leda is a river in north-western Germany in the state of Lower Saxony.
evidence.title: Leda (river)

evidence.text: It is a right tributary of the Ems and originates at the confluence of the Sagter Ems and the Soeste (Dreyschloot) near the town of Barßel.
evidence.title: Leda (river)

evidence.text: The Leda flows into the Ems near the town of Leer.
evidence.title: Leda (river)

evidence.text: The total length of the river is 29 km , of which the lower 1.9 km are navigable for sea-going vessels.
evidence.title: Leda (river)

evidence.text: German ("Deutsch" ] ) is a West Germanic language that is mainly spoken in Central Europe.
evidence.title: German language

evidence.text: It is the most widely spoken and (co-) official language in Germany, Austria, Switzerland, South Tyrol (Italy), the German-speaking Community of Belgium, and Liechtenstein.
evidence.title: German language

evidence.text: It is also one of the three official languages of Luxembourg.
evidence.title: German language

evidence.text: The languages which are most similar to German are the other members of the West Germanic language branch: Afrikaans, Dutch, English, the Frisian languages, Low German/Low Saxon, Luxembourgish, and Yiddish.
evidence.title: German language

evidence.text: German is the second most widely spoken Germanic language, after English.
evidence.title: German language

evidence.text: English is a West Germanic language that was first spoken in early medieval England and is now a global "lingua franca".
evidence.title: English language

evidence.text: Named after the Angles, one of the Germanic tribes that migrated to England, it ultimately derives its name from the Anglia (Angeln) peninsula in the Baltic Sea.
evidence.title: English language

evidence.text: It is closely related to the Frisian languages, but its vocabulary has been significantly influenced by other Germanic languages, particularly Norse (a North Germanic language), as well as by Latin and Romance languages, particularly French.
evidence.title: English language

evidence.text: Proto-Norse (also called Proto-Scandinavian, Primitive Norse, Proto-Nordic, Ancient Nordic, Ancient Scandinavian, Old Nordic, Old Scandinavian, Proto-North Germanic, North Proto-Germanic or Common Scandinavian) was an Indo-European language spoken in Scandinavia that is thought to have evolved as a northern dialect of Proto-Germanic in the first centuries CE.
evidence.title: Proto-Norse language

evidence.text: It is the earliest stage of a characteristically North Germanic language, and the language attested in the oldest Scandinavian Elder Futhark inscriptions, spoken around from the 2nd to 8th centuries (corresponding to the late Roman Iron Age and the Germanic Iron Age).
evidence.title: Proto-Norse language

evidence.text: It evolved into the dialects of Old Norse at the beginning of the Viking Age in about 800, which later themselves evolved into modern North Germanic languages.
evidence.title: Proto-Norse language

evidence.text: Dutch (   ) is a West Germanic language that is spoken by around 24 million people as a first language—including the population of the Netherlands and about sixty percent that of Belgium—and by another 5 million as a second language.
evidence.title: Dutch language

evidence.text: It is the third most widely spoken Germanic language, after English and German.
evidence.title: Dutch language

evidence.text: Afrikaans ( ) is a West Germanic language spoken in South Africa, Namibia and, to a lesser extent, Botswana and Zimbabwe.
evidence.title: Afrikaans

evidence.text: It evolved from the Dutch vernacular of South Holland (Hollandic dialect) spoken by the mainly Dutch settlers of what is now South Africa, where it gradually began to develop distinguishing characteristics in the course of the 18th century.
evidence.title: Afrikaans

evidence.text: Hence, it is a daughter language of Dutch, and was previously referred to as "Cape Dutch" (a term also used to refer collectively to the early Cape settlers) or "kitchen Dutch" (a derogatory term used to refer to Afrikaans in its earlier days).
evidence.title: Afrikaans

evidence.text: However, it is also variously described as a creole or as a partially creolised language.
evidence.title: Afrikaans

evidence.text: The term is ultimately derived from Dutch "Afrikaans-Hollands " meaning "African Dutch".
evidence.title: Afrikaans

question: Which was fought earlier in our nation's history, the Seven Days Battles or the Battle of Manila?

evidence.text: The Battle of Manila (February 3, 1945 – March 3, 1945) was a major battle of the Philippine campaign of 1944-45, during the Second World War.
evidence.title: Battle of Manila (1945)

evidence.text: It was fought by American and Filipino forces against Japanese troops in Manila, the capital city of the Philippines.
evidence.title: Battle of Manila (1945)

evidence.text: The month-long battle, which resulted in the death of over 100,000 civilians and the complete devastation of the city, was the scene of the worst urban fighting in the Pacific theater.
evidence.title: Battle of Manila (1945)

evidence.text: Japanese forces committed mass murder against Filipino civilians during the battle.
evidence.title: Battle of Manila (1945)

evidence.text: Along with massive loss of life, the battle also destroyed architectural and cultural heritage dating back to the city's foundation.
evidence.title: Battle of Manila (1945)

evidence.text: The battle ended the almost three years of Japanese military occupation in the Philippines (1942–1945).
evidence.title: Battle of Manila (1945)

evidence.text: The city's capture was marked as General Douglas MacArthur's key to victory in the campaign of reconquest.
evidence.title: Battle of Manila (1945)

evidence.text: The Battle of Cross Keys was fought on June 8, 1862, in Rockingham County, Virginia, as part of Confederate Army Maj. Gen. Thomas J. "Stonewall" Jackson's campaign through the Shenandoah Valley during the American Civil War.
evidence.title: Battle of Cross Keys

evidence.text: Together, the battles of Cross Keys and Port Republic the following day were the decisive victories in Jackson's Valley Campaign, forcing the Union armies to retreat and leaving Jackson free to reinforce Gen. Robert E. Lee for the Seven Days Battles outside Richmond, Virginia.
evidence.title: Battle of Cross Keys

evidence.text: The Battle of Gaines's Mill, sometimes known as the First Battle of Cold Harbor or the Battle of Chickahominy River, took place on June 27, 1862, in Hanover County, Virginia, as the third of the Seven Days Battles (Peninsula Campaign) of the American Civil War.
evidence.title: Battle of Gaines's Mill

evidence.text: Following the inconclusive Battle of Beaver Dam Creek (Mechanicsville) the previous day, Confederate General Robert E. Lee renewed his attacks against the right flank of the Union Army, relatively isolated on the northern side of the Chickahominy River.
evidence.title: Battle of Gaines's Mill

evidence.text: There, Brig. Gen. Fitz John Porter's V Corps had established a strong defensive line behind Boatswain's Swamp.
evidence.title: Battle of Gaines's Mill

evidence.text: Lee's force was destined to launch the largest Confederate attack of the war, about 57,000 men in six divisions.
evidence.title: Battle of Gaines's Mill

evidence.text: Porter's reinforced V Corps held fast for the afternoon as the Confederates attacked in a disjointed manner, first with the division of Maj. Gen. A.P. Hill, then Maj. Gen. Richard S. Ewell, suffering heavy casualties.
evidence.title: Battle of Gaines's Mill

evidence.text: The arrival of Maj. Gen. Stonewall Jackson's command was delayed, preventing the full concentration of Confederate force before Porter received some reinforcements from the VI Corps.
evidence.title: Battle of Gaines's Mill

evidence.text: Savage's Station was the wartime name of a supply depot, ammunition dump, field hospital, and command headquarters of the Army of the Potomac during the Peninsula Campaign of the American Civil War.
evidence.title: Savage's Station, Virginia

evidence.text: Savage's Station was located in Henrico County, Virginia on what was the Richmond and York River Railroad, however the historical department of the Norfolk Southern Railroad, the railroad track's current owner, has no record that an actual train station or station house ever existed on the property.
evidence.title: Savage's Station, Virginia

evidence.text: A farmhouse is known to have been located in a copse of trees on a small knoll next to the railroad track and is visible in several period drawings and photographs made during the war.
evidence.title: Savage's Station, Virginia

evidence.text: The house served as the nucleus of a large field hospital during and after the battle of Seven Pines and the Seven Days Battles.
evidence.title: Savage's Station, Virginia

evidence.text: The house also functioned as General George B. McClellan's headquarters during the battle of Savage's Station on June 29, 1862.
evidence.title: Savage's Station, Virginia

evidence.text: Although the house survived the battle in 1862, it was burned by Federal cavalry under General Philip H. Sheridan in 1864.
evidence.title: Savage's Station, Virginia

evidence.text: The house appears to have never been rebuilt, and no trace of it remains today.
evidence.title: Savage's Station, Virginia

evidence.text: However, a smokehouse from the 19th century still existed on the property as late as the 1930s when it was photographed during a survey of local historical structures as a project of the Civilian Conservation Corps.
evidence.title: Savage's Station, Virginia

evidence.text: The smokehouse fell into ruin and collapsed sometime prior to the 1980s.
evidence.title: Savage's Station, Virginia

evidence.text: A small brick-walled cemetery from the 18th century still sits near the former location of the house not far from the railroad track.
evidence.title: Savage's Station, Virginia

evidence.title: Battle of Port Republic

evidence.text: Port Republic was a fierce contest between two equally determined foes and was the most costly battle fought by Jackson's Army of the Valley during its campaign.
evidence.title: Battle of Port Republic

evidence.text: Together, the battles of Cross Keys (fought the previous day) and Port Republic were the decisive victories in Jackson's Valley Campaign, forcing the Union armies to retreat and leaving Jackson free to reinforce Gen. Robert E. Lee for the Seven Days Battles outside Richmond, Virginia.
evidence.title: Battle of Port Republic

evidence.text: The Seven Days Battles were a series of six major battles over the seven days from June 25 to July 1, 1862, near Richmond, Virginia, during the American Civil War.
evidence.title: Seven Days Battles

evidence.text: Confederate General Robert E. Lee drove the invading Union Army of the Potomac, commanded by Maj. Gen. George B. McClellan, away from Richmond and into a retreat down the Virginia Peninsula.
evidence.title: Seven Days Battles

evidence.text: The series of battles is sometimes known erroneously as the Seven Days Campaign, but it was actually the culmination of the Peninsula Campaign, not a separate campaign in its own right.
evidence.title: Seven Days Battles

evidence.text: The Northern Virginia Campaign, also known as the Second Bull Run Campaign or Second Manassas Campaign, was a series of battles fought in Virginia during August and September 1862 in the Eastern Theater of the American Civil War.
evidence.title: Northern Virginia Campaign

evidence.text: Confederate General Robert E. Lee followed up his successes of the Seven Days Battles in the Peninsula Campaign by moving north toward Washington, D.C., and defeating Maj. Gen. John Pope and his Army of Virginia.
evidence.title: Northern Virginia Campaign

evidence.text: The Battle of Malvern Hill, also known as the Battle of Poindexter's Farm, was fought on July 1, 1862 between the Confederate Army of Northern Virginia, led by Gen. Robert E. Lee, and the Union Army of the Potomac under Maj. Gen. George B. McClellan.
evidence.title: Battle of Malvern Hill

evidence.text: It was the final battle of the Seven Days Battles during the American Civil War, taking place on a 130 ft elevation of land known as Malvern Hill, near the Confederate capital of Richmond, Virginia and just one mile (1.6 km) from the James River.
evidence.title: Battle of Malvern Hill

evidence.text: Including inactive reserves, more than fifty thousand soldiers from each side took part, using more than two hundred pieces of artillery and three warships.
evidence.title: Battle of Malvern Hill

evidence.text: Divya S. Menon (born 14 March 1987) is an Indian singer and television anchor from Kerala.

evidence.text: She started her film career with Ee Pattanathil Bhootham.
evidence.title: Divya S. Menon

evidence.text: She was noticed by Shaan Rahman while anchoring music shows and picked her for Vineeth Sreenivasan - Shaan Rahman debut album, Coffee @ MG Road.
evidence.title: Divya S. Menon

evidence.text: She is associated with Blogswara and have sung in multiple albums in the series.
evidence.title: Divya S. Menon

evidence.text: Divya has sung in Vineeth Sreenivasan's super hit romantic movie, Thattathin Marayathu composed by Shaan Rahman.
evidence.title: Divya S. Menon

evidence.text: She has been associated with Vineeth - Shaan ventures, including Malarvadi Arts Club.
evidence.title: Divya S. Menon

evidence.text: In 2014 the hit wedding song "Thudakkham Maangalyam" from Anjali Menon's Bangalore Days gave her much popularity which she sang along with along with Vijay Yesudas and Sachin Warrier composed by Gopi Sunder.
evidence.title: Divya S. Menon

evidence.text: In 2015 Divya was noticed more promptly when she sang the song "Puthumazhayai" from Martin Prakkat's Charlie (2015 Malayalam film) composed by Gopi Sundar while the same song was sung by Shreya Ghoshal too.
evidence.title: Divya S. Menon

evidence.text: She also sang several ad jingles for various music composers both in Malayalam and Tamil.
evidence.title: Divya S. Menon
